title: Der kluge Knecht
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 162. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (muß, thu, thut).
about: KHM 162 is a brief, dry joke rather than a story: a servant sent to find a lost cow instead spends the day chasing three blackbirds and gives his master a straight-faced, nonsensical account of why that was time well spent. The narrator then turns to address the reader directly, urging them to take this servant as a model — a piece of irony aimed at anyone who shirks and dresses it up as wisdom, so read the closing 'moral' as mockery, not sincere advice.

sentences.t: Wie glücklich ist der Herr, und wie wohl steht es mit seinem Hause, wenn er einen klugen Knecht hat, der auf seine Worte zwar hört, aber nicht danach thut und lieber seiner eigenen Weisheit folgt.
sentences.l: How happy is the master, and how well it stands with his house, when he has a clever servant who does indeed listen to his words, but does not act by them and rather follows his own wisdom.
sentences.i: How fortunate is the master, and how well it goes with his household, when he has a clever servant who listens to his orders, to be sure, but does not act on them and prefers to follow his own wisdom.
sentences.n: The whole opening is ironic — the servant’s “cleverness” is doing the opposite of what he is told. “zwar … aber” = “indeed … but.” “thut” is 1857 for tut (does).

sentences.t: Ein solcher kluger Hans ward einmal von seinem Herrn ausgeschickt, eine verlorene Kuh zu suchen.
sentences.l: Such a clever Hans was once sent out by his master to look for a lost cow.
sentences.i: Such a clever Hans was once sent out by his master to search for a stray cow.
sentences.n: “ward” is the older past of werden (became/was), forming the passive “was sent out.” Hans is a stock name for the everyman fool, and is left untranslated.

sentences.t: Er blieb lange aus, und der Herr dachte „der treue Hans, er läßt sich in seinem Dienste doch keine Mühe verdrießen.“
sentences.l: He stayed away long, and the master thought, “faithful Hans — he lets no trouble in his service vex him.”
sentences.i: He was gone a long while, and the master thought, “good faithful Hans — he never lets any effort in his service put him off.”
sentences.n: “sich keine Mühe verdrießen lassen” is an idiom: not to let effort discourage one, to spare no pains. The master’s trust is misplaced — dramatic irony.

sentences.t: Als er aber gar nicht wiederkommen wollte, befürchtete der Herr es möchte ihm etwas zugestoßen sein, machte sich selbst auf und wollte sich nach ihm umsehen.
sentences.l: But as he would not come back at all, the master feared that something might have befallen him, set himself off and meant to look about for him.
sentences.i: But when he simply would not return, the master feared something might have happened to him, set out himself, and went to look for him.
sentences.n: “sich aufmachen” = to set out; “sich umsehen nach” = to look around for. “möchte … sein” is the subjunctive of reported fear, “might have befallen.”

sentences.t: Er mußte lange suchen, endlich erblickte er den Knecht, der im weiten Feld auf und ab lief.
sentences.l: He had to search long; at last he caught sight of the servant, who was running up and down in the open field.
sentences.i: He had to search a long time; at last he spied the servant running up and down in the open field.
sentences.n: “mußte” (1857) = musste, had to. “erblicken” = to catch sight of, spy.

sentences.t: „Nun lieber Hans,“ sagte der Herr, als er ihn eingeholt hatte, „hast du die Kuh gefunden, nach der ich dich ausgeschickt habe?“
sentences.l: “Now, dear Hans,” said the master, when he had caught up with him, “have you found the cow after which I sent you out?”
sentences.i: “Well now, dear Hans,” said the master once he had caught up with him, “have you found the cow I sent you out for?”
sentences.n: “einholen” = to catch up with, overtake. The relative “nach der” carries the “nach” of the idiom “to send out for something.”

sentences.t: „Nein, Herr,“ antwortete er, „die Kuh habe ich nicht gefunden, aber auch nicht gesucht.“
sentences.l: “No, sir,” he answered, “the cow I have not found — but neither have I looked for it.”
sentences.i: “No, sir,” he answered, “I have not found the cow — but then, I never looked for it.”
sentences.n: The fronted object “die Kuh” (the cow, first) throws the weight onto it; the deadpan “aber auch nicht gesucht” is the joke.

sentences.l: “What did you look for then, Hans?”
sentences.n: “denn” in a question is a flavouring particle — “then, pray,” mild curiosity — not the conjunction “for, because.”

sentences.t: „Etwas Besseres und das habe ich auch glücklich gefunden.“
sentences.l: “Something better — and that I have also happily found.”
sentences.i: “Something better — and that I duly found, too.”
sentences.n: “glücklich” here = successfully, happily (as in arriving safe and sound), keeping up the irony.
The master presses on; “das” points back to the “something better.”
“Amsel” = the blackbird, a thrush. The literal is already plain English, so no separate idiomatic line.

sentences.t: „Und wo sind sie?“ fragte der Herr.
sentences.l: “And where are they?” asked the master.
sentences.n: Still the master takes the servant seriously — the humour rides on his patience.

sentences.t: „Eine sehe ich, die andere höre ich und die dritte jage ich“ antwortete der kluge Knecht.
sentences.l: “One I see, the other I hear, and the third I chase,” answered the clever servant.
sentences.i: “One I can see, another I can hear, and the third I am chasing,” answered the clever servant.
sentences.n: The punch-line: he has “caught” none of the three — one seen, one heard, one still pursued. The fronted objects (“Eine … die andere … die dritte”) give the tally its rhythm.

sentences.t: Nehmt euch daran ein Beispiel, bekümmert euch nicht um euern Herrn und seine Befehle, thut lieber was euch einfällt und wozu ihr Lust habt, dann werdet ihr eben so weise handeln, wie der kluge Hans.
sentences.l: Take yourselves an example from this: do not trouble yourselves about your master and his orders; rather do what occurs to you and what you have a mind to, then you will act just as wisely as clever Hans.
sentences.i: Take a lesson from this: do not concern yourselves with your master and his commands; do rather whatever comes into your head and whatever you fancy, and you will act just as wisely as clever Hans.
sentences.n: The mock-moral, delivered straight-faced — the reader is meant to hear the opposite. “sich ein Beispiel an etwas nehmen” = to take something as an example; “Lust haben zu” = to feel like, have a mind to. “thut” = tut (do).

glossary.hört: hören — to hear, to heed (3rd sg.; auf seine Worte hört = heeds his words — NOT hört auf/stops)
glossary.weise: weise — wise (adj./adv.; so weise handeln = to act so wisely — NOT die Weise/manner)
